sdidlab

Synthetic difference-in-differences for a single treated unit, with the inference and diagnostics that design needs.

sdidlab is built around the synthdid estimator of Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens and Wager (2021). Where it reproduces synthdid, it does so exactly: point estimates, unit and time weights, and placebo standard errors match synthdid to machine precision, and the test suite enforces it. On top of that it adds:

  • Trimmed placebo inference. In a large, heterogeneous donor pool, many placebo draws are fitted badly and inflate the placebo standard error. placebo_se_trimmed() drops placebos whose pre-period fit is more than trim_k times worse than the treated unit’s. It trims the inference distribution, never the donor pool.
  • Fit diagnostics that respect SDID. SDID absorbs a constant level gap between the treated unit and its synthetic control, so trend_rmse measures the pre-period gap after removing its mean, on the covariate-adjusted outcome when covariates are used.
  • Two covariate routes. Hand covariates to synthdid, or residualise the outcome on untreated cells first (Kranz 2022) with project_out_covariates().
  • A bias-corrected synthetic control. fit_scm() implements the Abadie–Diamond–Hainmueller estimator with predictor matching, the Abadie–L’Hour bias correction, an optional Abadie–L’Hour penalty that makes the weights unique, and ranked-RMSPE permutation inference through scm_placebo_permutation() and rmspe_pvalue(). The weights are solved exactly by an active-set method, and an exact pre-period fit – where the weights, and therefore the estimate, are not unique – is flagged rather than silently resolved.

Installation

synthdid is not on CRAN, so install both from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("James-Hodges/sdidlab")

The Remotes field pins synthdid to the commit the parity tests were run against.

Example: California’s Proposition 99 

library(sdidlab)

data("california_prop99", package = "synthdid")
setup <- synthdid::panel.matrices(california_prop99)

set.seed(1)
fit <- fit_sdid(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, replications = 200, trim_k = 5)

fit$att                 # -15.6 packs per capita, as in Arkhangelsky et al.
c(fit$ci_lo, fit$ci_hi) # placebo-based 95% interval
fit$trend_rmse          # pre-period fit, level gap removed
fit$placebos_kept       # how many of the 200 placebos survived trimming

With trim_k = Inf the standard error is synthdid’s own placebo standard error, draw for draw under the same seed.

The synthetic-control alternative:

scm <- fit_scm(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, v_method = "mspe")
scm$att                 # bias-corrected ATT

perm <- scm_placebo_permutation(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, v_method = "mspe")
r <- perm$results
rmspe_pvalue(setNames(r$rmspe_ratio_raw, r$unit), r$att, r$unit[r$treated])

Workflow

For more than a one-off fit, describe each model as a specification and let sdidlab handle the bookkeeping:

panel <- prop99_panel()          # or sdid_panel(your_data, unit = , time = , outcome = )
spec  <- sdid_spec(label = "Prop 99", inference = list(replications = 200))
run   <- fit_spec(spec, panel, seed = seed_for(spec), store = "runs")

plot_sdid_trajectory(run)
plot_gap_path(run)
plot_placebo_distribution(run)

Specifications hash to a stable identifier, round-trip through YAML (one file can hold a whole robustness sweep), and fitted runs are saved so they can be reloaded and re-plotted without refitting. write_spec_script() writes a self-contained R script that reproduces every fit exactly.

run_demo() opens an interactive app that does all of this in the browser: build a specification, fit it, inspect every diagnostic, compare fits, and download the specifications and a reproducing script.

Validation

The test suite checks sdidlab against independent implementations, not just against itself:

What Checked against
SDID, SC and DiD estimates and weights synthdid, to 1e-12
Placebo standard errors (untrimmed), with and without covariates synthdid::vcov(method = "placebo"), to 1e-10 under the same seed
Covariate residualisation Two-way fixed-effects OLS on untreated cells, and fixest
Synthetic-control weights, plain and penalised The KKT optimality conditions; an independent long-run solve; Synth with the same V
Bias correction An independent per-period OLS computation

References

Abadie, A., Diamond, A. and Hainmueller, J. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies. Journal of the American Statistical Association 105(490), 493–505.

Abadie, A. and L’Hour, J. (2021). A Penalized Synthetic Control Estimator for Disaggregated Data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 116(536), 1817–1834.

Arkhangelsky, D., Athey, S., Hirshberg, D. A., Imbens, G. W. and Wager, S. (2021). Synthetic Difference-in-Differences. American Economic Review 111(12), 4088–4118.

Kranz, S. (2022). Synthetic Difference-in-Differences with Time-Varying Covariates. Working paper.
